ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: During the initial data collection, 182 participants were recruited from BYU and USF.
Participants were recruited from undergraduate psychology courses via each site's participant pool management system.
Participants provided written informed consent prior to study participation.
Therefore, additional participants were recruited from both sites using a two-phase approach.

First, participants were screened using the Achenbach Adult Self-Report (ASR; Achenbach et al., 2003), and those participants with T scores of 64 or higher on either the internalizing or externalizing composite subscales were invited for the second phase: the in-lab EEG recording.
table.formatted: First, participants were screened using the Achenbach Adult Self-Report (ASR; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Achenbach et al., 2003)</ref>, and those participants with T scores of 64 or higher on either the internalizing or externalizing composite subscales were invited for the second phase: the in-lab EEG recording.

table.text: During the additional data collection, 89 participants were recruited, resulting in a total of 271 participants.
This likely reflects that more participants were screened into the study based on elevated Internalizing Composite Scores than on elevated Externalizing Composite Scores.

Participants completed a modified version of the Eriksen flanker task (Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974), which lasted approximately 20 minutes and was presented using E-Prime Software (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA).
table.formatted: Participants completed a modified version of the Eriksen flanker task <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974)</ref>, which lasted approximately 20 minutes and was presented using E-Prime Software (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA).

table.text: Participants were seated 65 cm from the computer screen.
On each trial, participants were presented with five white arrowheads arranged horizontally.
Participants were instructed to press the left or right mouse button according to the direction of the central target arrow.

Participants were excluded if fewer than six error trials were retained after artifact correction and rejection, consistent with the exclusion criteria used in the parent study (Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.research_questions:
This preregistration is an update to an already posted registration (https://osf.io/39sfa). The original preregistration is attached for convenience.

Amendment to the Original Preregistration:
Internalizing and externalizing symptoms were examined as part of the parent project, and we identified a limited range of clinical symptoms on the Achenbach Adult Self Report (ASR) measure [ASR Internalizing Composite Scores (M=16.07, SD=10.61, IQR=8.00-22.00), ASR Externalizing Composite Scores (M=8.00, SD=5.58, IQR=4.00-10.50), ASR Anxious/Depressed Subscale (M=10.05, SD=6.67), ASR Withdrawn Subscale (M=3.38, SD=2.70), and ASR Somatic Complaints Subscale (M=2.64, SD=2.94)]. The restriction of range led to concern that the sample provided an inadequate range of symptoms for the dimensional analyses proposed in this preregistration. Therefore, we decided to postpone further data analysis until we complete recruitment for participants with higher symptom severity.

We plan to recruit a minimum of 60 participants up to a maximum of 100 participants with usable data across both sites. Data collection will stop once we have reached 100 participants with usable data or once we have reached 60 participants worth of usable data by May 1st, 2024. Participants will first complete the ASR online, and those participants with a scale score of 64 or greater on the internalizing or externalizing composite subscales will be invited for the in-lab EEG recording.

The approach to participant recruitment is the only adjustment for the preregistered protocol (https://osf.io/39sfa), and all in-lab procedures are identical to the preregistered protocol.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps > .05", Text = "ASR internalizing and externalizing symptom scores were positively correlated with each other, r(245) = .55, p < .001, but were not significantly correlated with ERP component amplitudes (|rs| ≤ .11, ps > .05)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "ps > .05", Sentence = "ASR internalizing and externalizing symptom scores were positively correlated with each other, r(245) = .55, p < .001, but were not significantly correlated with ERP component amplitudes (|rs| ≤ .11, ps > .05)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 341 columns across 8 data files.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: During the initial data collection, 182 participants were recruited from BYU and USF.
Participants were recruited from undergraduate psychology courses via each site's participant pool management system.
Participants provided written informed consent prior to study participation.
Therefore, additional participants were recruited from both sites using a two-phase approach.

First, participants were screened using the Achenbach Adult Self-Report (ASR; Achenbach et al., 2003), and those participants with T scores of 64 or higher on either the internalizing or externalizing composite subscales were invited for the second phase: the in-lab EEG recording.
During the additional data collection, 89 participants were recruited, resulting in a total of 271 participants.
This likely reflects that more participants were screened into the study based on elevated Internalizing Composite Scores than on elevated Externalizing Composite Scores.

Participants completed a modified version of the Eriksen flanker task (Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974), which lasted approximately 20 minutes and was presented using E-Prime Software (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA).
Participants were seated 65 cm from the computer screen.
On each trial, participants were presented with five white arrowheads arranged horizontally.
Participants were instructed to press the left or right mouse button according to the direction of the central target arrow.

Participants were excluded if fewer than six error trials were retained after artifact correction and rejection, consistent with the exclusion criteria used in the parent study (Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025).
Participants provided their parent or guardian's income if they were dependent on the parents or guardian who provided for them.
Participants completed the ASR as a measure of internalizing and externalizing symptoms.

#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

#### File paths

**8 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `gavs_resp.csv` to `Data for Registered Replication Report/gavs_resp.csv` (in RRR_ERN.Rmd); `gavs_stim.csv` to `Data for Registered Replication Report/gavs_stim.csv` (in RRR_ERN.Rmd); `ReliabilityTable.csv` to `Data for Registered Replication Report/ReliabilityTable.csv` (in RRR_ERN.Rmd); `rrr_ern_mtmm_expl_ern.rds` to `Data for Registered Replication Report/rrr_ern_mtmm_expl_ern.rds` (in RRR_ERN.Rmd); `rrr_ern_mtmm_expl_pe.rds` to `Data for Registered Replication Report/rrr_ern_mtmm_expl_pe.rds` (in RRR_ERN.Rmd); `rrr_ern_mtmm_expl_n2.rds` to `Data for Registered Replication Report/rrr_ern_mtmm_expl_n2.rds` (in RRR_ERN.Rmd); `rrr_ern_mtmm_expl_n1.rds` to `Data for Registered Replication Report/rrr_ern_mtmm_expl_n1.rds` (in RRR_ERN.Rmd); `erpbx_alldata.Rdata` to `erpbx_alldata.RData` (in RRR_ERPBx.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 2 references matched several files sharing a name and could not be resolved by study group or folder; they were left unrewritten and flagged.

**1 file name in the code is not the same as in the deposit**, in case, spaces or punctuation, and exactly one file in the deposit fits. To run the code we corrected this in a copy of the script so that it finds the file. The script itself should be changed, because as written it does not find the file on every system.

1 file only defines functions, so running it on its own says nothing: a function counts when a script uses it. These files are not counted as scripts. 0 are used by no script in the deposit.

#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 9 scripts: 2 ran without error, 4 errored, 0 timed out, 2 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with `source()`. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **2 scripts could not be tried, because a file they need was not downloaded**: overall_dependability.R, task_comparisons_ICC_dependability.R. They are not counted as scripts that did not reproduce. The file: Data for Psychometric Reliability of ERN and Pe Across Flanker Stroop and GoNo-Go Tasks-  A Direct and Conceptual Replication/output_ern_0int.rds (955.8 MB); files over 100 MB are not downloaded. **1 script stopped on a file another script writes**, so it was run once more after the other scripts: `RRR_ERN.Rmd` (rrr_ern_alldata.RData). One file was written in another folder than where the script looked, so before that run we copied it there: `Archive of OSF Storage/Data for Registered Replication Report/rrr_ern_alldata.RData` to `rrr_ern_alldata.RData` for `RRR_ERN.Rmd`. The scripts assume they all run from one folder; saying which, or building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), solves this. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_).

**2 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

**Run by another script**

1 script is run by another script with `source()`, so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script's outcome.

text.text: Performance monitoring involves evaluating actions and adjusting behavior accordingly.

Atypical neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring are commonly observed in individuals with psychopathology, raising the possibility that psychiatric symptoms may disrupt the link between error-related neural activity and subsequent behavioral adjustment.
However, neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring are often examined separately, leaving trial-level event-related brain potential (ERP) coupling with behavior poorly understood.

The present study examined whether previous-trial error-related ERP components predicted currenttrial behavior (i.e., response time [RT], accuracy) and whether these relationships varied by selfreported internalizing and externalizing symptoms.
In a college student sample (N=247), larger previous-trial error-related negativity (ERN), an index of early error monitoring, predicted longer RTs.
In contrast, larger previous-trial error positivity (Pe), an index of later error awareness, predicted higher current-trial accuracy in the confirmatory model.
Internalizing and externalizing symptom scores did not robustly moderate these ERP-behavior relationships or consistently predict behavioral adjustments.

These findings suggest that trial-level coupling between errorrelated ERP components and behavioral adjustment showed no robust evidence of differing across levels of self-reported internalizing and externalizing symptoms within the observed range.
More broadly, the results highlight the value of examining performance monitoring as an integrated neural-behavioral process rather than as isolated neural or behavioral indices.

Cognitive dysfunction is increasingly conceptualized as a transdiagnostic feature of psychopathology (Abramovitch et al., 2021; Etkin et al., 2013; Romer & Pizzagalli, 2021; Semkovska et al., 2019), and cognitive functioning is closely tied to everyday functioning and quality of life (Bonnín et al., 2019; Bruijnen et al., 2019; Burton et al., 2019; Liddle, 2019; Weightman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Cognitive dysfunction is increasingly conceptualized as a transdiagnostic feature of psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Abramovitch et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Etkin et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">Romer & Pizzagalli, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Semkovska et al., 2019)</ref>, and cognitive functioning is closely tied to everyday functioning and quality of life <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bonnín et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bruijnen et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Burton et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Liddle, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">Weightman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Performance monitoring is a critical part of everyday cognitive function and supports the evaluation and regulation of behavior.

Atypical patterns in the neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring are observed across psychiatric symptoms and traditional diagnostic categories, suggesting that disruptions in both neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring may be linked to mental health and illness (Clayson, 2025; Delfin et al., 2020; Hall et al., 2007; Hoyniak & Petersen, 2019; Lee et al., 2020; Pasion et al., 2023; Riesel et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Atypical patterns in the neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring are observed across psychiatric symptoms and traditional diagnostic categories, suggesting that disruptions in both neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring may be linked to mental health and illness <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Clayson, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Delfin et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Hall et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Hoyniak & Petersen, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Lee et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Pasion et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Riesel et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, neural and behavioral measures are often examined separately, which makes it difficult to determine whether psychiatric symptoms are linked to disruptions in neural responses to errors, altered behavioral adjustment, or disrupted coupling between error-related neural activity and subsequent behavior.

This distinction matters because preserved neural-behavior coupling would suggest that error-monitoring signals continue to guide behavioral adjustment even when neural or behavioral indices appear atypical, whereas weakened coupling would suggest a more fundamental disruption in the performance-monitoring system.

The present study, therefore, tested whether trial-level error-related neural activity predicted subsequent behavioral adjustment and whether this neural-behavioral coupling varied across internalizing and externalizing symptom severity.
Event-related brain potentials (ERPs) are direct, noninvasive measures of neural activity that are often used to study performance monitoring in healthy and clinical populations.

The error-related negativity (ERN) is a negative deflection in the scalp-recorded ERP with a frontocentral scalp distribution that peaks within 100ms after error commission (Falkenstein et al., 1991; Gehring et al., 1993) and is an index of performance monitoring that is related to posterror adjustments in behavior (Larson et al., 2014; Weinberg et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The error-related negativity (ERN) is a negative deflection in the scalp-recorded ERP with a frontocentral scalp distribution that peaks within 100ms after error commission <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Falkenstein et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Gehring et al., 1993)</ref> and is an index of performance monitoring that is related to posterror adjustments in behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Larson et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Weinberg et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Although accounts of ERN's precise functional significance differ (Clayson, Kappenman, et al., 2021), prevailing explanations converge on the view that ERN indexes early error detection and reflects activity of a performance-monitoring system that supports behavioral adjustments in line with the goals of a task (Botvinick et al., 2001; Eysenck et al., 2023; Falkenstein et al., 1991; Gehring et al., 1993; Kieffaber et al., 2023; Larson et al., 2012; LoTemplio et al., 2023; Yeung et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Although accounts of ERN's precise functional significance differ <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Clayson, Kappenman, et al., 2021)</ref>, prevailing explanations converge on the view that ERN indexes early error detection and reflects activity of a performance-monitoring system that supports behavioral adjustments in line with the goals of a task <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Botvinick et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Eysenck et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Falkenstein et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Gehring et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Kieffaber et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Larson et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">LoTemplio et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Yeung et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The error positivity (Pe) is another index of performance monitoring that reflects later stages of error processing.

Pe is a slow positive-going deflection in the scalp-recorded ERP with a centroparietal scalp distribution that peaks between 200 and 400ms after error commission (S. Nieuwenhuis et al., 2001; Overbeek et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Pe is a slow positive-going deflection in the scalp-recorded ERP with a centroparietal scalp distribution that peaks between 200 and 400ms after error commission (S. <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Nieuwenhuis et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Overbeek et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Theories on the functional significance of Pe posit that it reflects attentional orientation to unexpected events (i.e., errors) following automatic inhibition after errors (Desender et al., 2021; Wessel, 2018).
text.formatted: Theories on the functional significance of Pe posit that it reflects attentional orientation to unexpected events (i.e., errors) following automatic inhibition after errors <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Desender et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">Wessel, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence supports that Pe represents a manifestation of a performance monitoring system that serves to adapt behaviors following error commission (Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011; Overbeek et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Evidence supports that Pe represents a manifestation of a performance monitoring system that serves to adapt behaviors following error commission <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Overbeek et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Together, ERN and Pe provide complementary markers of early and later stages of error processing.
A defining feature of performance monitoring is that recent performance can shape subsequent behavior.

Post-error slowing, defined as longer response times (RTs) following errors than following correct responses, is robust across tasks and samples (Dutilh et al., 2011; Li et al., 2022; Rabbitt & Rodgers, 1977; Schroder & Moser, 2014).
text.formatted: Post-error slowing, defined as longer response times (RTs) following errors than following correct responses, is robust across tasks and samples <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Dutilh et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Li et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">Rabbitt & Rodgers, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">Schroder & Moser, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: While several studies reported larger ERN or Pe predicted post-error slowing (Carp & Compton, 2009; Hajcak et al., 2003; Lutz et al., 2026; Schroder et al., 2020; Steinhauser & Andersen, 2019), other studies failed to observe such relationships (Buzzell et al., 2017; Núñez Castellar et al., 2010; Gehring & Fencsik, 2001).
text.formatted: While several studies reported larger ERN or Pe predicted post-error slowing <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carp & Compton, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Hajcak et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Lutz et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Schroder et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">Steinhauser & Andersen, 2019)</ref>, other studies failed to observe such relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Buzzell et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">Núñez Castellar et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Gehring & Fencsik, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Findings for the relationship between ERN/Pe and post-error accuracy are similarly mixed (Forster & Cho, 2014).
text.formatted: Findings for the relationship between ERN/Pe and post-error accuracy are similarly mixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Forster & Cho, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Earlier work likewise found that relationships between response-locked performance-monitoring ERPs and behavioral indices depended on the ERP component and performance measure examined (Larson & Clayson, 2011).
text.formatted: Earlier work likewise found that relationships between response-locked performance-monitoring ERPs and behavioral indices depended on the ERP component and performance measure examined <ref type="bibr">(Larson & Clayson, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: These inconsistencies suggest that ERP-behavior relationships may depend on moderating factors (Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011; Volpert-Esmond et al., 2018), analytic approaches (Park et al., 2024; Park et al., 2025), and individual differences.
text.formatted: These inconsistencies suggest that ERP-behavior relationships may depend on moderating factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Volpert-Esmond et al., 2018)</ref>, analytic approaches <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Park et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Park et al., 2025)</ref>, and individual differences.

text.text: Altered post-error behavioral adjustments in psychiatric disorders may reflect disruption in performance monitoring, raising the possibility that psychiatric symptoms moderate the coupling between previous-trial ERN/Pe and current-trial behavior (Hall et al., 2007; Klein et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Altered post-error behavioral adjustments in psychiatric disorders may reflect disruption in performance monitoring, raising the possibility that psychiatric symptoms moderate the coupling between previous-trial ERN/Pe and current-trial behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Hall et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Klein et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: If psychiatric symptoms alter the efficiency or consistency with which error-related neural activity guides subsequent behavior, then symptom severity should be associated not only with ERP amplitudes or behavioral indices considered separately, but also with the strength of triallevel ERP-behavior coupling.

Additionally, statistical methods used to analyze neural and behavioral data likely contribute to mixed findings for relationships between ERN/Pe and behavioral adjustments (Clayson et al., 2022; Clayson, Shuford, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Additionally, statistical methods used to analyze neural and behavioral data likely contribute to mixed findings for relationships between ERN/Pe and behavioral adjustments <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Clayson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Clayson, Shuford, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Studies have typically examined between-person differences in subject average scores, but focusing on subject-average scores ignores intraindividual differences in the means and variances of neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring (Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011; Volpert-Esmond et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Studies have typically examined between-person differences in subject average scores, but focusing on subject-average scores ignores intraindividual differences in the means and variances of neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">Volpert-Esmond et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: If psychiatric symptoms are associated with instability in performance monitoring or inconsistency in translating error detection into behavior, those effects are unlikely to be detected with between-person correlations of averaged scores.
Trial-level analyses that preserve within-person covariation are therefore necessary to evaluate whether symptoms relate to altered ERP-behavior coupling.
Error-related ERPs have been linked to psychopathology at both categorical and dimensional levels, although effects vary across symptom domains, tasks, and samples.

Larger ERN is most consistently reported across individuals with anxiety-related and obsessivecompulsive disorders (Cavanagh et al., 2010; Holmes & Pizzagalli, 2010; Klawohn et al., 2020), whereas blunted ERN is often observed across disorders characterized by problems with inhibitory control or behavioral problems, such as substance use disorders (Euser et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2023), attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; Herrmann et al., 2010), and psychosis (Martin et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Larger ERN is most consistently reported across individuals with anxiety-related and obsessivecompulsive disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cavanagh et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Holmes & Pizzagalli, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Klawohn et al., 2020)</ref>, whereas blunted ERN is often observed across disorders characterized by problems with inhibitory control or behavioral problems, such as substance use disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Euser et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Liu et al., 2023)</ref>, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Herrmann et al., 2010)</ref>, and psychosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Martin et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Dimensional findings show similar patterns: Higher internalizing symptom scores were associated with larger (i.e., more negative) ERN (Moser et al., 2013; Riesel, 2019; Vaidyanathan et al., 2012), whereas smaller ERN was found to be associated with higher externalizing symptom scores (Hall et al., 2007; Martin et al., 2018; Pasion & Barbosa, 2019).
text.formatted: Dimensional findings show similar patterns: Higher internalizing symptom scores were associated with larger (i.e., more negative) ERN <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">(Moser et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Riesel, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">Vaidyanathan et al., 2012)</ref>, whereas smaller ERN was found to be associated with higher externalizing symptom scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Hall et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Martin et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Pasion & Barbosa, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analytic work further suggests that Pe may be elevated in samples characterized by anxiety-or obsessive-compulsive features and reduced in samples characterized by antisocial or behavioral problems (Bellato et al., 2021; Lutz et al., 2021; Vallet et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Meta-analytic work further suggests that Pe may be elevated in samples characterized by anxiety-or obsessive-compulsive features and reduced in samples characterized by antisocial or behavioral problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bellato et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Lutz et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">Vallet et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, ERP findings indicate that excessive or attenuated responses to errors appear related to dimensions of internalizing and externalizing symptoms.
Behavioral indices of performance monitoring also differ across psychiatric symptoms, although their functional interpretation is not straightforward.

Many studies report prolonged post-error RTs in internalizing-related conditions, whereas diminished or absent post-error slowing is more often reported in externalizing-related conditions characterized by disinhibition (Balogh & Czobor, 2016; Kofler et al., 2013; Sullivan et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Many studies report prolonged post-error RTs in internalizing-related conditions, whereas diminished or absent post-error slowing is more often reported in externalizing-related conditions characterized by disinhibition <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Balogh & Czobor, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Kofler et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">Sullivan et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, post-error slowing can show weak or inconsistent relations with improvements in accuracy, complicating functional interpretations of longer RTs as adaptive (Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011; Li et al., 2021; Wessel, 2018).
text.formatted: However, post-error slowing can show weak or inconsistent relations with improvements in accuracy, complicating functional interpretations of longer RTs as adaptive <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Danielmeier & Ullsperger, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Li et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">Wessel, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Considering the unique relationship between psychiatric symptoms and atypical behavioral adjustments, further examination of post-error behavioral adjustments in relation to other performance monitoring indices is needed to explain how psychiatric symptoms may contribute to disturbances in behavioral adjustments.
Evidence of dissociations between neural and behavioral indices further motivates a coupling-based approach.

For example, abnormal enhancements in ERN were found in OCD, yet clinical group differences in post-error behavioral adjustment were not observed, suggesting relatively intact behavioral performance despite overactive error monitoring (Endrass et al., 2010).
text.formatted: For example, abnormal enhancements in ERN were found in OCD, yet clinical group differences in post-error behavioral adjustment were not observed, suggesting relatively intact behavioral performance despite overactive error monitoring <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Endrass et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, a blunted ERN was found in people with ADHD, but clinical group differences were not observed for post-error RTs (Ehlis et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Conversely, a blunted ERN was found in people with ADHD, but clinical group differences were not observed for post-error RTs <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Ehlis et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Dimensional work suggests that symptom-related differences in ERPs can emerge even when behavioral differences are small or absent (Compton et al., 2008; Hsieh et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Dimensional work suggests that symptom-related differences in ERPs can emerge even when behavioral differences are small or absent <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Compton et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Hsieh et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These dissociations raise the possibility that psychiatric symptoms affect the translation of error-related neural activity into subsequent behavior, an effect that is poorly captured by analyses of averaged scores.
Multilevel location-scale models (MLSMs) provide a framework to identify systematic changes in neural and behavioral indices at the trial level.

MLSMs can simultaneously estimate fixed and random effects for the conditional means (location) and variances (scale), the latter of which is not modeled in traditional location-only multilevel models (Walters et al., 2018).
text.formatted: MLSMs can simultaneously estimate fixed and random effects for the conditional means (location) and variances (scale), the latter of which is not modeled in traditional location-only multilevel models <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">(Walters et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction is important because psychiatric symptoms may be associated with slower or less accurate responding on average and with greater inconsistency in how neural responses to performance are translated into subsequent behavior.

MLSMs facilitate the analysis of withinperson variance in the data that might fluctuate as a function of categorical and dimensional covariates (e.g., individual differences, event type, psychiatric symptom scores, etc.; Volpert-Esmond et al., 2021).
text.formatted: MLSMs facilitate the analysis of withinperson variance in the data that might fluctuate as a function of categorical and dimensional covariates (e.g., individual differences, event type, psychiatric symptom scores, etc.; <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">Volpert-Esmond et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: MLSMs have been successfully applied to studies of ERP components (Clayson et al., 2022; Clayson, Rocha, et al., 2024; Heindorf et al., 2025; Holbrook, Park, Baldwin, et al., 2025; Holbrook, Park, Rast, et al., 2025; Park et al., 2024; Park et al., 2025), making them well-suited to evaluating symptom-related heterogeneity in performancemonitoring dynamics.
text.formatted: MLSMs have been successfully applied to studies of ERP components <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Clayson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Clayson, Rocha, et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Heindorf et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Holbrook, Park, Baldwin, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Holbrook, Park, Rast, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Park et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">Park et al., 2025)</ref>, making them well-suited to evaluating symptom-related heterogeneity in performancemonitoring dynamics.

text.text: For instance, trial-level MLSMs showed that within-person ERP-behavior relationships can remain intact even when clinical group differences in ERP amplitudes or behavioral indices are present (Park et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For instance, trial-level MLSMs showed that within-person ERP-behavior relationships can remain intact even when clinical group differences in ERP amplitudes or behavioral indices are present <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Park et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Such findings demonstrate the value of separating questions about average-level differences from questions about within-person neuralbehavioral coupling.

The present study used trial-level data to test whether previous-trial error-related ERPs predict current-trial behavior and whether internalizing and externalizing symptom dimensions moderate within-person ERP-behavior relationships.
This approach was intended to clarify whether internalizing and externalizing symptoms are linked to altered translation of neural error processing into post-error behavioral adaptation.
It was hypothesized that larger ERN and larger Pe following errors would predict longer RTs and higher accuracy on the current trial.
It was further hypothesized that higher internalizing and externalizing symptom scores would be associated with weaker ERP-behavior coupling.

Lastly, exploratory model comparisons evaluated alternative MLSM specifications to identify the combination of previous-trial ERP, symptom, and experimental predictors that best accounted for changes in current-trial RT and accuracy.
The present study used data from a multi-site registered replication study (https://osf.io/8cbua/) to test the proposed hypotheses (Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: The present study used data from a multi-site registered replication study (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/8cbua/">https://osf.io/8cbua/</ref>) to test the proposed hypotheses <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The two sites involved in the study were Brigham Young University (BYU) in Provo, UT, USA and the University of South Florida (USF) in Tampa, FL, USA.

Additional data were collected at both sites using the same protocol as the original data collection approach, except that the recruitment plan aimed to enrich the sample with participants high in internalizing and externalizing symptoms (see Participants section).
The original study examined the convergent and discriminant validity of ERN, Pe, and other ERP components recorded during different tasks.
The original study did not examine whether psychiatric symptom scores moderated the relationships between ERN/Pe and behavioral performance.
During the initial data collection, 182 participants were recruited from BYU and USF.
Participants were recruited from undergraduate psychology courses via each site's participant pool management system.
Participants provided written informed consent prior to study participation.

Exclusion criteria were assessed via self-report and included difficulty understanding written and spoken English, uncorrected visual impairment, history of head injury (e.g., loss of consciousness for more than 10 minutes) or neurological disease (e.g., craniocerebral trauma, meningitis, stroke, epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, brain tumor, or migraines more often than four times per month), and age younger than 18 or older than 65 years.

Participants in the parent dataset showed a restricted range of self-reported internalizing and externalizing symptoms, limiting sensitivity to test the present moderation hypotheses (Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Participants in the parent dataset showed a restricted range of self-reported internalizing and externalizing symptoms, limiting sensitivity to test the present moderation hypotheses <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, additional participants were recruited from both sites using a two-phase approach.

First, participants were screened using the Achenbach Adult Self-Report (ASR; Achenbach et al., 2003), and those participants with T scores of 64 or higher on either the internalizing or externalizing composite subscales were invited for the second phase: the in-lab EEG recording.
text.formatted: First, participants were screened using the Achenbach Adult Self-Report (ASR; <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Achenbach et al., 2003)</ref>, and those participants with T scores of 64 or higher on either the internalizing or externalizing composite subscales were invited for the second phase: the in-lab EEG recording.

text.text: This threshold applied only to the supplemental recruitment and did not require elevated scores on both composites.
A T score of 64 is 1.4 normative standard deviations above the mean of 50.
The final dataset combined the original and supplemental samples.
Aside from this adjustment in the recruitment procedure, the additional data collection adhered to the research protocol of the original data collection.

The additional data collection aimed to recruit a minimum of 60 to 100 participants with usable data across both sites, yielding a planned total sample size of at least 242 participants (preregistration for the additional data is publicly available: https://osf.io/4et8h/overview).
text.formatted: The additional data collection aimed to recruit a minimum of 60 to 100 participants with usable data across both sites, yielding a planned total sample size of at least 242 participants (preregistration for the additional data is publicly available: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/4et8h/overview">https://osf.io/4et8h/overview</ref>).

text.text: The sample size of the supplemental data collection was constrained by available recruitment resources (Lakens, 2022).
text.formatted: The sample size of the supplemental data collection was constrained by available recruitment resources <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">(Lakens, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, the final sample was larger than the typical sample size of 29 (SD = 21) reported in typical studies of ERPs (Clayson et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, the final sample was larger than the typical sample size of 29 (SD = 21) reported in typical studies of ERPs <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Clayson et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: During the additional data collection, 89 participants were recruited, resulting in a total of 271 participants.

Of those participants, ten were excluded because they did not have EEG and behavioral data for the flanker task, six were excluded due to corrupted recording files, and eight were excluded based on the a priori data-processing exclusion criteria (i.e., fewer than six error trials retained after artifact correction and rejection).
The final study sample size was 247 participants.

Internal consistency of ERP data was estimated using dependability coefficients () from generalizability theory and is reported in Table 1 (Baldwin et al., 2015; Clayson, 2020 Clayson, , 2024;; Clayson, 2025; Clayson, Baldwin, et al., 2021; Clayson & Miller, 2017a , 2017b; Rocha et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Internal consistency of ERP data was estimated using dependability coefficients () from generalizability theory and is reported in Table 1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Baldwin et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Clayson, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Clayson, , 2024;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Clayson, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Clayson, Baldwin, et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Clayson & Miller, 2017a</ref> <ref type="bibr">, 2017b;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">Rocha et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: High internal consistency has been reported for the Internalizing and Externalizing composite scores in a sample of American adults (𝛼s > .80).
text.formatted: High internal consistency has been reported for the Internalizing and Externalizing composite scores in a sample of American adults (𝛼s > .80).

text.text: Composite T scores from the Internalizing and Externalizing scales were used as the primary symptom measures.

The range of self-reported symptom scores in the final dataset was broader than in the original sample for the Internalizing Composite Scores (M=56.22, SD=11.64, IQR=48-64, range = 30-85) but remained restricted for Externalizing Composite Scores (M=48.84, SD=8.81, IQR=43-54, range = 30-70).
This likely reflects that more participants were screened into the study based on elevated Internalizing Composite Scores than on elevated Externalizing Composite Scores.
Internalizing and externalizing symptom scores demonstrated good internal consistency (αs = .92 and .84, respectively).

Participants completed a modified version of the Eriksen flanker task (Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974), which lasted approximately 20 minutes and was presented using E-Prime Software (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA).
text.formatted: Participants completed a modified version of the Eriksen flanker task <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Eriksen & Eriksen, 1974)</ref>, which lasted approximately 20 minutes and was presented using E-Prime Software (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA).

text.text: Participants were seated 65 cm from the computer screen.
The task comprised seven blocks of 60 trials each, resulting in a total of 420 trials, in which the order of trials was randomly determined within each block.
Twenty practice trials were presented at the beginning of the task.

During the task, stimuli were displayed for a duration of 200ms on a black background, followed by a jittered inter-trial interval (ITI) that randomly varied between 600 and 1,000ms (uniform distribution).
On each trial, participants were presented with five white arrowheads arranged horizontally.

The arrows either all pointed in the same direction (congruent trial; >>>>>, <<<<<) or had the central target arrow pointing in the opposite direction of the flanking arrows (incongruent trial; <<><<, >><>>).
text.formatted: The arrows either all pointed in the same direction (congruent trial; >>>>>, <<<<<) or had the central target arrow pointing in the opposite direction of the flanking arrows (incongruent trial; <<><<, >><>>).

text.text: Participants were instructed to press the left or right mouse button according to the direction of the central target arrow.
Each trial block comprised 50% congruent and 50% incongruent trials.
At a viewing distance of 65 cm, the arrow array occupied 2 degrees of visual angle vertically and 10 degrees horizontally.
After each block, performance-based feedback was provided to emphasize both speed and accuracy of the responses.
If the block accuracy was below 75%, the feedback "Please try to be more accurate" was presented.
Conversely, if block accuracy was above 90%, the feedback "Please try to respond faster" was provided.
For block accuracy between 75% and 90%, the feedback "You're doing a great job" was given.
Electroencephalographic (EEG) data were recorded at BYU and USF from 128 Ag/AgCl passive scalp sites using a geodesic sensor net and Electrical Geodesics, Inc.
(EGI; Eugene, OR) Net Amps 400 amplifier system (20K nominal gain, delta-sigma sinc lowpass filter with a halfpower cutoff of 2,000 Hz).
The sensor layout of the net can be found in Clayson et al. (2012).
text.formatted: The sensor layout of the net can be found in <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Clayson et al. (2012)</ref>.

text.text: EEG was initially referenced to the vertex electrode and digitized continuously at 500Hz with a 24-bit analog-to-digital converter.
Impedances were maintained below 50 kΩ.
Data processing steps were similar to those used in the original study of the registered replication report to maintain comparability of study findings (Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Data processing steps were similar to those used in the original study of the registered replication report to maintain comparability of study findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Continuous EEG was rereferenced to an algebraic link of two channels: TP9 and TP10, corresponding to mastoids.

Then continuous data were filtered using a fourth-order (24 dB/octave) infinite impulse response (IIR) Butterworth filter, with half-amplitude cutoffs at 0.10 and 30 Hz, implemented in ERPLab v8.02 (Lopez-Calderon & Luck, 2014).
text.formatted: Then continuous data were filtered using a fourth-order (24 dB/octave) infinite impulse response (IIR) Butterworth filter, with half-amplitude cutoffs at 0.10 and 30 Hz, implemented in ERPLab v8.02 <ref type="bibr">(Lopez-Calderon & Luck, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Response-locked ERPs were segmented individually for each participant, spanning a temporal window from 400ms prior to the participant's button press to 800ms following the button press.

Activity associated with eye blinks and horizontal and vertical saccadic eye movements was then removed from the segmented waveforms using independent components analysis (ICA) implemented in the ERP PCA Toolkit v2.95 (Dien, 2010).
text.formatted: Activity associated with eye blinks and horizontal and vertical saccadic eye movements was then removed from the segmented waveforms using independent components analysis (ICA) implemented in the ERP PCA Toolkit v2.95 <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Dien, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Epoched EEG data from all channels were processed through a binary version of EEGLab's runica function called binica (Delorme & Makeig, 2004).
text.formatted: Epoched EEG data from all channels were processed through a binary version of EEGLab's runica function called binica <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Delorme & Makeig, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: ICA components were removed if their scalp topography correlated at .9 or higher with a blink template or at .8 or higher with vertical or horizontal saccade templates.
The templates that were used for artifact correction included those automatically generated by the ERP PCA Toolkit and those created from collected data (Dien, 2010).
text.formatted: The templates that were used for artifact correction included those automatically generated by the ERP PCA Toolkit and those created from collected data <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Dien, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Movement artifacts were removed using temporal principal component analysis (PCA) with a promax rotation that identifies factors accounting for amplitude differences greater than 200μV within a trial (Dien, 2010).
text.formatted: Movement artifacts were removed using temporal principal component analysis (PCA) with a promax rotation that identifies factors accounting for amplitude differences greater than 200μV within a trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Dien, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Channels with an absolute correlation with the nearest six neighboring channels that fell below .4 were marked as globally bad.

On a trial-wise basis, channels with a voltage range exceeding 100μV within an epoch, channels that were flat, and channels with more than a 30μV difference with the nearest six neighbors were marked as bad for the epoch.
Channels that were marked as bad for more than 20% of epochs were considered globally bad.
Bad channels were interpolated using spherical splines (Perrin et al., 1989), but if more than 10% of channels were marked bad for an epoch, the entire epoch was rejected.
text.formatted: Bad channels were interpolated using spherical splines <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">(Perrin et al., 1989)</ref>, but if more than 10% of channels were marked bad for an epoch, the entire epoch was rejected.

text.text: Participants were excluded if fewer than six error trials were retained after artifact correction and rejection, consistent with the exclusion criteria used in the parent study (Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Participants were excluded if fewer than six error trials were retained after artifact correction and rejection, consistent with the exclusion criteria used in the parent study <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Response-locked ERPs were baseline adjusted using a time window from 400ms to 200ms before the participant's response.
ERN was quantified at the trial level using a timewindow mean amplitude from 0 to 100ms following participant response at electrode site 6 (FCz).
Pe was similarly quantified at the trial level using a time-window mean amplitude from 200 to 400ms at electrode 62 (Pz).
Multilevel models were used to examine relationships between trial-level ERP scores and behavior.
For RT, MLSMs were used to model both mean RT and RT variability.
For accuracy, multilevel Bernoulli outcome models were used because accuracy was binary.

MLSMs facilitate the examination of average scores (location portion of the model) and within-person variance (scale portion of the model; the scale portion modeled standard deviations using a log link).
These models have been successfully implemented in studies of trial-level ERP scores (Clayson, Brush, et al., 2021; Clayson et al., 2022; Clayson, Shuford, et al., 2024).
text.formatted: These models have been successfully implemented in studies of trial-level ERP scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Clayson, Brush, et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Clayson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Clayson, Shuford, et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: By relaxing the assumption of a homogeneous variance structure, MLSMs support the modeling of residual variance as a function of covariates, which is essential for testing the proposed hypotheses.
The proposed analyses examined the same predictors on the location and scale portions of the model.

Predictors on the location portion of the model aimed to clarify the degree to which previoustrial ERN amplitude, previous-trial Pe amplitude, and internalizing or externalizing symptoms predicted current-trial behavior.
Predictors on the scale portion of the model aimed to clarify the degree to which predictors accounted for changes in the variability of behavior.
The models for testing each hypothesis are described below using Wilkinson notation (Wilkinson & Rogers, 1973).
text.formatted: The models for testing each hypothesis are described below using Wilkinson notation <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">(Wilkinson & Rogers, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: In the following notation, Behavior represents either current-trial RT or accuracy, depending on the model, and ERN and Pe represent ERP component amplitudes from the previous trial.
Internalizing and Externalizing represent the composite scores centered on each dimension for the given individual.
Random effects were included for Previous Trial and Subject to account for ERP component amplitudes being nested within previous trials, which were nested within participants.
Of note, all interaction effects include lower-order constituent main effects.
Separate models were used to examine RTs and accuracy.

Data were included in the trial-level models only when the previous trial had ERP component scores retained and the current trial had valid behavioral data (i.e., a response was required for the RT analysis; trials with no response were retained in the accuracy analysis and coded as errors).
The first trial of each block was excluded because it did not have a preceding trial.

This model parallels the typical analysis of post-error behavioral adjustments and helps to determine whether previous-trial ERP components relate to current-trial behavior, ignoring any effect of psychiatric symptoms.

Previous-trial accuracy (Rabbitt & Rodgers, 1977) and current-trial congruency (Kornblum et al., 1990) were included to account for the effect of experimental conditions and previous-trial performance that may impact currenttrial behavior.

text.text: Exploratory Analysis.

Exploratory model comparisons were conducted to identify the combination of previous-trial ERP component amplitudes, symptoms, and interaction variables that best predicted current-trial RT and accuracy.
To limit the model search space, all candidate models included current-trial congruency and previous-trial accuracy.
Candidate models then varied in whether they included previous-trial ERN, previous-trial Pe, Internalizing, Externalizing, and the theoretically relevant ERP-symptom interactions.
Models were constructed such that interaction terms always included their lower-order terms.
The same fixed-effect structure was used in the location and scale portions of RT models.
A total of 47 candidate models was evaluated for each outcome. using the package brms v2.20.4 (Bürkner, 2017), which is a front-end wrapper for Stan (Stan Development Team, 2021).

text.text: For the models with RTs as the dependent variable, the prior for the intercept on the location portion of the model used a normal distribution with a mean of 500 and a standard deviation of 100, and the priors for the fixed effects used a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 100.
Variance components were estimated using a Student's t prior distribution with 10 degrees of freedom, a location parameter of 0, and a scale parameter of 2.
A Lewandowski-Kurowicka-Joe (LKJ) prior distribution with a shape parameter of 2 was used as the prior for the correlation matrices of the group-level effects (Lewandowski et al., 2009).

text.text: The prior is defined over positive-definite correlation matrices for the group-level effects.
A shape = 2 parameter can be considered mildly informative, placing more weight on an identity matrix.
For the model with accuracy as the dependent variable, Bayesian location-only multilevel models with Bernoulli outcomes (0 [error], 1 [correct]) were used and fit with a logit link.
In such analyses, there was no scale portion of the model to estimate.
A flat prior was used for the population-level intercept and population-level regression coefficients.
An LKJ prior distribution with a shape parameter of 1 was used as the prior for the correlation between the varying intercepts, and a shape = 1 parameter can be considered a uniform prior.
Leave-one-out cross-validation via Pareto smoothed importance sampling (LOO-CV) was used to compare model fit using the loo package in R (Vehtari et al., 2017).

text.text: Model comparisons were performed using LOO-CV, which compares the predictive accuracy of the models.
The following criteria were used to identify the optimal model.

1) The difference in expected log predictive density was greater than 4.2) The difference in expected log predictive density was greater than 2 times the standard error of the difference in expected log predictive density.

When the above criteria did not identify a single best-fitting model, the model with the fewest predictors among those not distinguishable from the model with the highest expected log predictive density under these criteria was selected.
When model comparison did not favor a more complex model, parameter estimates from that model were treated as descriptive and were not interpreted as robust evidence for the corresponding hypothesis.

The first hypothesis would be supported if the 95% credible intervals (CrIs) of the posterior samples for the 1) parameter estimates of previous-trial ERN were negative and excluded 0 and 2) parameter estimates of previous-trial Pe were positive and excluded 0 for the model predicting current-trial RTs and the model predicting current-trial accuracy.

This finding would support the conclusion that greater (i.e., more negative) previous-trial ERN and larger (i.e., more positive) previous-trial Pe predict longer RTs and improved current-trial accuracy.

The second hypothesis would be supported 1) if Model 2 showed improved model fit over Model 1 using LOO-CV and 2) if the 95% CrIs of the posterior samples for the parameter estimates of the interaction effects (ERN x Internalizing, ERN x Externalizing, Pe x Internalizing, Pe x Externalizing) excluded 0 for the model predicting current-trial RTs and the model predicting current-trial accuracy; the parameter estimates for the interaction effects should be in the direction toward smaller effects (e.g., positive estimates for interactions with ERN and negative estimates for interactions with Pe).
This finding would support the conclusion that greater psychiatric symptom scores are associated with weaker relationships between previoustrial error-monitoring ERPs and current-trial behavior.
For the exploratory analysis, models were compared using LOO-CV, and the optimal model was identified using the rules described in the Model Comparison section.

If multiple models show the best predictive accuracy with the same number of predictors, the model with the numerically best expected log predictive density (i.e., least negative expected log predictive density) was selected as the optimal model for further interpretation.

text.text: RT Models Hypothesis 1.
The parameter estimates of the RT model for Hypothesis 1 are presented in Table 4.

A larger previous-trial ERN (i.e., more negative) predicted longer current-trial RTs but did not predict current-trial RT variability (location 95% credible interval [CrI] [-.17, -.03]; scale 95% CrI [-.002, 0.00003]).
Specifically, each 1-µV increase in previous-trial ERN (i.e., a more negative ERN) was associated with a current-trial RT that was 0.10 ms longer.
In contrast, larger previous-trial Pe (i.e., more positive) predicted neither current-trial RT nor its variability (location 95% CrI [-.07, 0.06]; scale 95% CrI [-.001, 0.0002]).

With respect to the experimental effects, RT was longer and more variable following error trials than correct trials (location 95% CrI [-17.25, -11.99]; scale 95% CrI [-.12, -.07]) and on current-incongruent trials than on current-congruent trials (location 95% CrI [-45.85, -40.49]; scale 95% CrI [-.23, -.19]).

In other words, RT was 14.57 ms longer when the previous trial was an error trial than when it was a correct trial; likewise, RT was 43.25 ms longer when the current trial was incongruent than congruent.
Overall, previous-trial ERN, but not Pe, predicted current-trial RT.
Therefore, Hypothesis 1 was partially supported for RT.
The effects of previous-trial ERN on current-trial RT and its variability are demonstrated in Figures 2 and 3, respectively.
text.formatted: The effects of previous-trial ERN on current-trial RT and its variability are demonstrated in Figures <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">3</ref>, respectively.

text.text: Hypothesis 2.
The parameter estimates of the RT model for Hypothesis 2 are presented in Table 5.
text.formatted: The parameter estimates of the RT model for Hypothesis 2 are presented in Table <ref type="table">5</ref>.

text.text: The model comparisons indicated that the model from Hypothesis 2 (i.e., model including the moderating role of psychiatric symptom scores) showed comparable fit to the model from Hypothesis 1 (i.e., without psychiatric symptom scores; differences in 𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= -1.24, SEs of 𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑑𝑖𝑓𝑓 ̂= 4.64).
Therefore, the more parsimonious model for Hypothesis 1 was interpreted, and Hypothesis 2 was not supported.
A total of 47 RT models were compared.
The LOO-CV comparison identified seven models that met the prespecified model-comparison criteria, which included the model from Hypothesis 1.
Among the seven models, the model from Hypothesis 1 included the fewest predictors and was consequently selected as the best-fitting model (i.e., ∆𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= -1.24, SE of ∆𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= 4.64).
The model interpretation is identical to that provided for the model in Hypothesis 1.
Taken together, exploratory RT models provided consistent evidence that more negative previous-trial ERN amplitudes predicted longer current-trial RTs.

Symptom terms did not improve predictive accuracy in the exploratory model-comparison framework, suggesting that ERP-RT relationships were broadly similar across levels of internalizing and externalizing symptom scores.
Interim Summary.
In summary, the RT models consistently showed that larger previous-trial ERN amplitudes predicted longer current-trial RTs.
Previous-trial Pe did not robustly predict current-trial RT or RT variability.
Internalizing and externalizing symptom scores did not meaningfully predict RT and did not provide robust evidence of moderation of ERP-RT associations.
Thus, Hypothesis 1 was partially supported for RT, and Hypothesis 2 was not supported.
The plots demonstrating the interactions between previous-trial ERPs and psychiatric symptom scores on current-trial RT are included in the supplementary materials.
Accuracy Models Hypothesis 1.
Parameter estimates of the accuracy model for Hypothesis 1 are presented in Table 6.

Larger previous-trial Pe predicted higher odds of a correct response on the current trial (odds ratio [OR] = 1.003, 95% CrI [1.0002, 1.005]; accuracy-model estimates are reported on the log-odds scale).
In other words, for each 1-µV increase in previous-trial Pe, the odds of observing a correct response on the subsequent trial increased by approximately 0.3%.
Previoustrial ERN did not predict current-trial accuracy (95% CrI [-.005, 0.001]).

Current-trial congruency predicted current-trial accuracy: accuracy was higher on congruent than incongruent trials, and the odds of a correct response were approximately 5.4 times greater on congruent than incongruent trials (OR = 5.40; 95% CrI [4.81, 6.17]).
Previous-trial accuracy did not predict current-trial accuracy (95% CrI [-.15, 0.11]).
Thus, Hypothesis 1 was partially supported for accuracy: previous-trial Pe, but not ERN, predicted current-trial accuracy.
The effect of previous-trial Pe on current-trial accuracy is demonstrated in Figure 4.
Hypothesis 2.
The parameter estimates of the accuracy model for Hypothesis 2 are presented in Table 7.

The model comparisons indicated that the model from Hypothesis 1 (i.e., without psychiatric symptom scores) showed indistinguishable fit compared to the model from Hypothesis 2 (i.e., the model including the moderating role of psychiatric symptom scores), while including fewer predictors (differences in 𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= -2.83, SEs of differences in 𝑒𝑙𝑝𝑑 𝑙𝑜𝑜 ̂= 1.52).
Therefore, the model from Hypothesis 1 was preferred, and Hypothesis 2 was not supported.
A total of 47 accuracy models were compared.

Although LOO-CV reduces the risk of selecting an overfit model by evaluating out-of-sample predictive performance, comparing a large number of candidate models in this exploratory analysis increases the possibility that the selected model capitalized on characteristics of the present data.
Therefore, the selected model should be interpreted cautiously, and its findings require independent replication in future studies.
Parameter estimates for the selected exploratory model are presented in Taken together, most predictors in the selected exploratory model had 95% credible intervals that included zero.
It is important to note that LOO-CV evaluates the predictive performance of the model as a whole rather than the evidence for individual parameters.

Hence, the selected model had the best out-of-sample predictive performance among the candidate models, even though there was limited posterior support for the associations between the individual predictors and current-trial accuracy.
