text.text: The present study examined whether previous-trial performance-monitoring ERP components predicted current-trial behavior and whether these relationships were moderated by self-reported psychiatric symptom severity.
Larger previous-trial ERN predicted longer currenttrial mean RTs, and larger previous-trial Pe predicted greater odds of a correct current-trial response in the confirmatory model.
In confirmatory analyses, internalizing and externalizing symptom terms did not improve predictive accuracy or provide robust evidence of moderation.
Internalizing and externalizing symptom terms did not improve predictive accuracy or provide robust evidence of moderation.
Taken together, these findings provide no robust evidence that broad ASR internalizing or externalizing symptom scores disrupted trial-level ERP-behavior coupling.
ERN-RT relationships were observed across different RT models, such that larger ERN (i.e., more negative) on the previous trial predicted longer mean RTs on the current trial.
This pattern of effects suggests that a heightened neural response to errors is associated with slower responding on the subsequent trial.
This relationship between larger ERN and longer RT is broadly consistent with other work (Carp & Compton, 2009; Hajcak et al., 2003; Mattes et al., 2022; Park et al., 2024; Schroder et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This relationship between larger ERN and longer RT is broadly consistent with other work <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Carp & Compton, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Hajcak et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Mattes et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Park et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Schroder et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: However, ERN-RT associations without meaningful ERN-accuracy associations at the trial level challenge the cognitive control account of the ERN, which holds that it reflects increased cognitive control following an error, thereby supporting the remedial action of error commission (Botvinick et al., 2001; Falkenstein et al., 1991; Gehring et al., 1993; Yeung et al., 2004).
text.formatted: However, ERN-RT associations without meaningful ERN-accuracy associations at the trial level challenge the cognitive control account of the ERN, which holds that it reflects increased cognitive control following an error, thereby supporting the remedial action of error commission <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Botvinick et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Falkenstein et al., 1991;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Gehring et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">Yeung et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: One of the prevailing accounts of post-error slowing posits that the delayed response may stem from momentary inhibition of ongoing motor activity or from heightened error processing that interferes with the reorientation of attention to the current trial (Houtman & Notebaert, 2013; Lavro et al., 2018; Wessel, 2018).
text.formatted: One of the prevailing accounts of post-error slowing posits that the delayed response may stem from momentary inhibition of ongoing motor activity or from heightened error processing that interferes with the reorientation of attention to the current trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Houtman & Notebaert, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Lavro et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">Wessel, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, such interference may impact encoding of the current-trial stimulus, which further impedes engagement with the current trial (Buzzell et al., 2017; Notebaert et al., 2009).
text.formatted: For instance, such interference may impact encoding of the current-trial stimulus, which further impedes engagement with the current trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Buzzell et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Notebaert et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: A pattern of longer RT following errors and an association between more negative previous-trial ERN amplitudes and longer current-trial RTs is consistent with orienting or interference accounts.
However, the absence of a clear ERN-accuracy relationship does not conclusively indicate that slowing was maladaptive or distinguish these accounts from adaptive adjustments.
It is important to note that the interpretation of post-error slowing and the ERN varies with the specifics of the experimental paradigms used.
Specifically, ERN amplitude is sensitive to prolonged task performance (Clayson, Baldwin, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Specifically, ERN amplitude is sensitive to prolonged task performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Clayson, Baldwin, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, larger ERN was found under experimental conditions where accuracy was emphasized over speed (Mattes et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Similarly, larger ERN was found under experimental conditions where accuracy was emphasized over speed <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Mattes et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The interpretation of post-error slowing also differs across task specifications, especially with respect to the response-stimulus interval (RSI).

Specifically, Wessel (2018) explains that posterror slowing during experimental paradigms with longer RSI may reflect increased caution, whereas post-error slowing during paradigms with shorter RSI may better reflect reorientation of attention following disengagement from an error.
text.formatted: Specifically, <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">Wessel (2018)</ref> explains that posterror slowing during experimental paradigms with longer RSI may reflect increased caution, whereas post-error slowing during paradigms with shorter RSI may better reflect reorientation of attention following disengagement from an error.

text.text: In summary, the present findings leave the functional significance of the ERN-RT association unresolved.

Examination of ERN-RT relationships across different experimental paradigms might help clarify the role of the errormonitoring process indexed by the ERN in the context of post-error behavioral adjustments.
In the confirmatory model, larger previous-trial Pe predicted greater odds of a correct response on the current trial.
However, this association was not retained as a robust effect in the exploratory model-comparison framework, so the Pe-accuracy finding should be interpreted cautiously.
The Pe coefficient remained positive in the exploratory model, but its 95% credible interval included zero.
Because that model included a Pe × Internalizing interaction, its Pe coefficient represented the association at a centered internalizing score of zero.
On the other hand, previous-trial ERN did not predict current-trial accuracy in any of the models.

Taken together, considering that ERN reflects rapid, automatic error detection that can trigger behavioral adjustment, whereas Pe reflects later conscious error awareness that may support a more strategic behavioral adjustment, it is plausible that deeper error processing, as indexed by a larger Pe, predicts improved accuracy in line with the task goal (Di Gregorio et al., 2018; Nieuwenhuis et al., 2001; Steinhauser & Yeung, 2010).
text.formatted: Taken together, considering that ERN reflects rapid, automatic error detection that can trigger behavioral adjustment, whereas Pe reflects later conscious error awareness that may support a more strategic behavioral adjustment, it is plausible that deeper error processing, as indexed by a larger Pe, predicts improved accuracy in line with the task goal <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Di Gregorio et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Nieuwenhuis et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">Steinhauser & Yeung, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: However, this functional interpretation remains tentative because evidence for a robust Pe-accuracy association was not consistent across model specifications.
Taken together, the findings are consistent with partially dissociable ERP-behavior associations, with the most robust evidence for an association between previous-trial ERN and current-trial RT.
Evidence for a Pe-accuracy association was more model-dependent.

Future work incorporating drift-diffusion modeling could clarify whether ERN-related RT slowing reflects increased response caution, changes in nondecision time, reduced processing efficiency, or other decision-related mechanisms (Grabowska et al., 2025; Mattes et al., 2022; Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008).

text.text: Examining the relationship between previous-trial ERPs and current-trial driftdiffusion model paramters could clarify how error-related neural activity relates to changes in response styles or efficiency of extracting information.

In confirmatory analyses, psychiatric symptom terms did not improve predictive accuracy under the prespecified model-comparison criteria, and the exploratory models did not provide robust evidence that symptom scores predicted behavior or moderated ERP-behavior associations.
These findings do not establish equivalent ERP-behavior relationships across symptom levels.
Supplemental recruitment broadened the observed internalizing range but did not comparably extend the externalizing range.
Limited representation of high externalizing scores may have reduced sensitivity to moderation and constrained generalization to populations with elevated externalizing symptoms.
Therefore, further investigation in samples spanning a broader distribution of externalizing severity is needed to determine whether externalizing symptoms show a moderating ERP-behavior effect.

Despite the limited literature on the ERP-behavior relationships in psychopathology, the present finding is consistent with a recent study that examined ERP-behavior relationships in people with psychosis and healthy comparison participants, where intact trial-level ERP-RT relationships were observed in both groups despite overall blunted ERPs in the psychosis group (Park et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Despite the limited literature on the ERP-behavior relationships in psychopathology, the present finding is consistent with a recent study that examined ERP-behavior relationships in people with psychosis and healthy comparison participants, where intact trial-level ERP-RT relationships were observed in both groups despite overall blunted ERPs in the psychosis group <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">(Park et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, the findings do not support the hypothesis that broad symptom severity disrupts these trial-level associations within the observed symptom range.

This is notable because studies in individuals with high internalizing or externalizing symptom severity often focused on symptom-or group-related differences in ERP component amplitudes (Lutz et al., 2021; Pasion & Barbosa, 2019; Riesel et al., 2017), whereas the present study tested whether symptom severity altered trial-level associations between ERP amplitudes and subsequent behavior.
text.formatted: This is notable because studies in individuals with high internalizing or externalizing symptom severity often focused on symptom-or group-related differences in ERP component amplitudes <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Lutz et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">Pasion & Barbosa, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Riesel et al., 2017)</ref>, whereas the present study tested whether symptom severity altered trial-level associations between ERP amplitudes and subsequent behavior.

text.text: In the present sample, however, exploratory participant-level correlations did not clearly reproduce typical symptom-ERP amplitude patterns, which may be due to differences in symptom breadth, task context, or scoring conventions.
The null findings for the moderating role of psychiatric symptoms may partly reflect the broad nature of the symptom measures used in the present study.
Atypical ERP-RT relationships might be more strongly related to specific symptom dimensions than to broad symptom clusters.

For example, although large ERN is often observed in internalizing psychopathology, potentiated ERN is typically observed in the context of OCD (Bellato et al., 2021; Hajcak et al., 2019; Riesel, 2019; Riesel et al., 2017), whereas findings in depression are mixed (Clayson et al., 2020; Hajcak et al., 2025; Klawohn et al., 2020; Weinberg et al., 2012).
text.formatted: For example, although large ERN is often observed in internalizing psychopathology, potentiated ERN is typically observed in the context of OCD <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bellato et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Hajcak et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">Riesel, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">Riesel et al., 2017)</ref>, whereas findings in depression are mixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Clayson et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Hajcak et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Klawohn et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">Weinberg et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, studies of behavioral measures suggest that changes in post-error RT might be more specific to particular disorders or symptoms than to broad internalizing symptoms (Rueppel et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Similarly, studies of behavioral measures suggest that changes in post-error RT might be more specific to particular disorders or symptoms than to broad internalizing symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">(Rueppel et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: One possibility is that ERP-behavior abnormalities are more closely tied to specific symptom profiles, diagnoses, or information-processing styles than to broad internalizing and externalizing composite scores (Kotov et al., 2021).
text.formatted: One possibility is that ERP-behavior abnormalities are more closely tied to specific symptom profiles, diagnoses, or information-processing styles than to broad internalizing and externalizing composite scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Kotov et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies that directly sample these profiles are needed to test this possibility.
For instance, future studies could compare validated hierarchical symptom models that distinguish shared psychopathology from more specific symptom dimensions (Caspi et al., 2014).
text.formatted: For instance, future studies could compare validated hierarchical symptom models that distinguish shared psychopathology from more specific symptom dimensions <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Caspi et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Such analyses would require evaluation of the measurement structure and the psychometric reliability and interpretation of the resulting factors.
The extraction of a general factor should not be assumed to reveal ERP-behavior relationships obscured by composite scores.
Taken together, the findings provide no robust evidence that broad internalizing or externalizing symptom scores moderated ERP-behavior associations in this undergraduate sample.
However, because clinical diagnoses were not evaluated in this sample, it is possible that findings would differ in a clinical sample.

Additionally, given the high comorbidity of psychopathology and the limited specificity captured by broad symptom clusters, future studies might examine different symptom profiles or maladaptive information processing styles that are closely tied to impaired cognitive control (Koster et al., 2017; Miyake et al., 2000; Owens et al., 2021; Owens et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Additionally, given the high comorbidity of psychopathology and the limited specificity captured by broad symptom clusters, future studies might examine different symptom profiles or maladaptive information processing styles that are closely tied to impaired cognitive control <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Koster et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Miyake et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Owens et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Owens et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The present study is not without its limitations.
First, the undergraduate sampling frame and supplemental recruitment strategy constrained the range and distribution of psychiatric symptom severity, particularly for externalizing symptoms.
Despite this limitation, the present study identified a robust trial-level ERN-RT relationship.
Replication in clinical populations is important to clarify how the performance monitoring system might be perturbed across varying levels and profiles of psychiatric symptom severity.
Second, ERP-behavior relationships were examined only during a flanker task.

Neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring, as well as their interrelationships, are known to show task-specific effects (Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025; Clayson et al., 2022; Park et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Neural and behavioral indices of performance monitoring, as well as their interrelationships, are known to show task-specific effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Clayson, McDonald, et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Clayson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Park et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, specific psychiatric symptom scores might play a role in the relationship between ERPs and behavior measured during other experimental tasks, as these measures in isolation appear to have different relations to measures of psychiatric symptoms across tasks (Gillan et al., 2016; Giordano et al., 2021; Weinberg et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Therefore, specific psychiatric symptom scores might play a role in the relationship between ERPs and behavior measured during other experimental tasks, as these measures in isolation appear to have different relations to measures of psychiatric symptoms across tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Gillan et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Giordano et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Weinberg et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, given that different information processing styles appear associated with impaired cognitive control in psychopathology (i.e., reflective rumination vs. depressive rumination; Koster et al., 2017; Miyake et al., 2000; Owens et al., 2021; Owens et al., 2025), the perturbed link between performance monitoring ERPs and behavior might be more pronounced when assessed during experimental tasks that target specific psychological processes of interest (e.g., social reward task, Distefano et al., 2018; Balloon Analogue Risk Task, Lejuez et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Moreover, given that different information processing styles appear associated with impaired cognitive control in psychopathology (i.e., reflective rumination vs. depressive rumination; <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Koster et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Miyake et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">Owens et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Owens et al., 2025)</ref>, the perturbed link between performance monitoring ERPs and behavior might be more pronounced when assessed during experimental tasks that target specific psychological processes of interest (e.g., social reward task, <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Distefano et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Balloon Analogue Risk Task, Lejuez et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Because the most consistent and robust effects emerged for RT, computational decomposition of RTs may provide mechanistic insight into which aspects of decision processing are related to error-monitoring ERP components.
RT is measured at the end of multiple layers of cognitive processes involved in decision making.
As a result, analyses of raw RT may provide only a coarse index of how error monitoring relates to subsequent goal-directed behavior (Dutilh et al., 2011; Weindel et al., 2021).
text.formatted: As a result, analyses of raw RT may provide only a coarse index of how error monitoring relates to subsequent goal-directed behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Dutilh et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">Weindel et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Drift diffusion modeling (DDM) is a computational model that facilitates decomposing RT into different cognitive parameters, such as response caution, response bias, and efficiency of information processing (Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008; Smith & Ratcliff, 2024).
text.formatted: Drift diffusion modeling (DDM) is a computational model that facilitates decomposing RT into different cognitive parameters, such as response caution, response bias, and efficiency of information processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">(Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">Smith & Ratcliff, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Given the preserved ERP-RT relationships observed in the present study and in other work on psychopathology (Park et al., 2025), linking error-monitoring ERPs from the previous trial to DDM parameters on the subsequent trial may help clarify how the errormonitoring system differentially drives behavioral adjustment across levels and types of psychiatric symptoms.

text.text: Last, the reported models also did not explicitly include trial-number trends or serially correlated residuals.
Consequently, the extent to which slow changes in attention, fatigue, or performance contributed to the lagged ERP-behavior associations remains unresolved.
Future studies might examine the role of the number of trials and task duration to delineate how ERPbehavior relations change over time, especially as a function of fatigue or habituation.
Despite these limitations, the present study had many strengths.
First, the sample size was relatively large for an EEG study (Clayson et al., 2019; Lakens, 2022).
text.formatted: First, the sample size was relatively large for an EEG study <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Clayson et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">Lakens, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Second, the use of triallevel multilevel models facilitated examination of within-person associations between performance-monitoring ERP component amplitudes and subsequent behavior, allowing the study to test lagged, within-person ERP-behavior associations rather than relying on participantlevel averages.

As such, the present study provides a foundation for studies that examine the dynamic relationships among different subcomponents of performance monitoring, and more broadly, cognitive control, by integrating multiple neural and behavioral measurements at the trial level.

Thus, the confirmatory Hypothesis 1 model provided evidence that larger previous-trial Pe predicted higher current-trial accuracy, but this association was not retained as a robust effect in the exploratory model-comparison framework.
Internalizing and externalizing symptoms did not robustly moderate ERP-accuracy relationships.
The plots demonstrating the interactions between previous-trial ERPs and psychiatric symptom scores on current-trial accuracy are included in the supplementary materials.

present study tested whether trial-level performance-monitoring ERP component amplitudes predicted subsequent behavior and whether these associations varied across broad internalizing and externalizing symptom scores.
Larger previous-trial ERN amplitudes predicted longer current-trial mean RTs, suggesting that stronger early error-monitoring activity was associated with slower responding on the next trial.
Larger previous-trial Pe amplitudes predicted greater odds of a correct current-trial response in the confirmatory model.

Internalizing and externalizing symptom scores did not provide robust evidence of moderation, indicating that broad ASR symptom severity did not robustly alter trial-level ERP-behavior associations within the observed symptom range of this undergraduate sample.
These findings highlight the value of examining performance monitoring as a trial-level neural-behavioral process rather than relying only on isolated ERP or behavioral averages.
